acceptable.choice: Build online cancellations in the existing Flask/Postgres codebase, as a separate change from any concurrency work
acceptable.why: The feature is ordinary CRUD with state changes and needs no new technology, and keeping it separate stops a risky runtime change hiding inside a feature PR.

acceptable.choice: Switch gunicorn to gevent workers (with psycogreen or a gevent-compatible Postgres driver, and monkey-patching checked)
acceptable.why: At 600 rps a 200–600 ms insurer call means about 120–360 requests waiting at once, and gevent lets a few processes hold hundreds of waiting calls while the team keeps writing Flask the same way.

acceptable.choice: Switch to gunicorn gthread workers (for example a few processes × 25–50 threads)
acceptable.why: The insurer wait is I/O, so the GIL doesn't matter, and threads are the smallest, best-understood change for a Flask team, as long as the code is thread-safe.

acceptable.choice: Scale sync workers horizontally across more containers as a short-term bridge, with PgBouncer in front of Postgres
acceptable.why: It needs no code change, but roughly 400+ processes means real memory cost and far more DB connections than Postgres allows by default, so it buys time at best.

acceptable.choice: Strict timeouts, bounded retries and a circuit breaker or bulkhead on the insurer call, plus a shared, pooled HTTP session
acceptable.why: At 600 rps a slow insurer would otherwise fill every worker and take down booking and cancellation together during the morning rush.

acceptable.choice: Load-test at 600+ rps against a stubbed insurer with realistic latency before the go-live month
acceptable.why: The new worker model, worker counts and connection limits have to be proven with measurements, not argued on paper.

acceptable.choice: Short-TTL caching of eligibility results, if the insurer and the business allow it
acceptable.why: It can cut calls to the insurer a lot, but only where eligibility doesn't need to be real-time.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the service in FastAPI/Starlette/asyncio before next month
ruled_out.why: A full rewrite of a healthcare booking API in a few weeks is a reliability risk, and gevent or gthread solve the waiting problem without it.

ruled_out.choice: Moving to Go, Node or another non-Python stack
ruled_out.why: The team wants to stay in Python, and it is unnecessary for an I/O-bound workload.

ruled_out.choice: Keeping the current 17 sync workers unchanged
ruled_out.why: By Little's law, 600 rps × about 0.4 s means roughly 240 requests in flight, against a capacity of 17. The rush would queue and time out.

ruled_out.choice: Adding Flask `async def` views under sync gunicorn workers as the fix
ruled_out.why: Flask runs each async view in its own event loop inside the worker, which still blocks for the whole request, so concurrency doesn't change.

ruled_out.choice: Shipping cancellations and ignoring the capacity issue
ruled_out.why: It breaks the team's main concern, reliability during the morning rush, which the new load will break first.

ruled_out.choice: Quietly switching the worker model inside the cancellations work
ruled_out.why: It overrides a documented team decision without discussion and mixes a runtime change with feature work.

must_mention: The documented decision to stay on sync workers rested on 40 rps; at 600 rps that premise is gone, and the team should revisit the decision explicitly (and record the new one) before the regional rollout.
Do the capacity math: 600 rps × 0.2–0.6 s ≈ 120–360 requests waiting at once, against 17 workers today, so the current setup will fail at peak.
Raise this before starting on cancellations, but still deliver cancellations; the two are separate pieces of work and the capacity work is more urgent.

Recommend gevent or gthread workers as the low-change fix that stays in Python, with the caveats: database driver compatibility with gevent (psycopg2 needs psycogreen), thread safety for gthread, and monkey-patching order.
Postgres connections: hundreds of concurrent requests or workers need a pool or PgBouncer, or max_connections runs out.
Protect the insurer dependency with timeouts, a circuit breaker and graceful degradation, and check whether the insurer can handle about 600 rps or will rate-limit.
Load-test at the expected peak before go-live.

Cancellations need correct domain handling: atomic state transitions or row locks against concurrent booking and cancel races, idempotent cancel requests, cancellation-window policy rules, freeing the slot, an audit trail suitable for healthcare, and notifying the patient (and the insurer, if needed).
Check whether cancellation calls the insurer, which would add to the same bottleneck.
red_flags: Implementing cancellations without mentioning the 15× load increase and the blocking insurer call.
Recommending a rewrite to FastAPI, Quart or another language on a one-month timeline.
Calling gevent drop-in without warning about blocking C extensions such as psycopg2 and monkey-patching.
Claiming Flask async views fix the problem under sync workers.
Recommending 'just add more workers' without accounting for memory and Postgres connection limits.
Unilaterally overriding the team's written decision, or dismissing it as wrong when it was right at 40 rps.
Adding retries on the insurer call without timeouts or backoff, which multiplies load during an insurer slowdown.
Caching eligibility indefinitely, or without checking that it is clinically and contractually acceptable.
Cancellation logic without concurrency control, idempotency or an audit trail.
Presenting performance numbers as fact without saying a load test is needed.
unknowns: The insurer's capacity, rate limits and SLA at about 600 rps, and its p99 latency (not just 200–600 ms).
Whether the cancellation flow calls the insurer or other external services.
Memory per gunicorn worker, and how far the containers or cluster can scale out.
Postgres max_connections, current pooling, and how much database work each request does.
The Postgres driver and HTTP client in use, and whether any C extensions or global state would break under gevent or threads.
The shape of the peak: sustained 600 rps or short spikes, and the overall share of booking versus cancellation traffic.
Whether eligibility results can legally and contractually be cached, and for how long.
Cancellation business rules: cutoff windows, fees, who may cancel, and what notifications are required.
